claims.text: The starting material is AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock.
Multi-scale modeling of thermal and mechanical behavior will be used to optimize additive-manufacturing process parameters.
Process-parameter optimization through multi-scale computational modeling can reduce residual thermal stresses.
Process-parameter optimization through multi-scale computational modeling can improve mechanical properties by 15% relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Optimizing additive-manufacturing parameters computationally is the mechanism responsible for the predicted property improvement.
Thermal and mechanical properties constitute the structural mediator between modeling-based optimization and the outcome.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions are the comparison baseline.
The magnitude of mechanical-property improvement may depend on the particular process parameters and material properties.
Metal additive manufacturing, particularly selective laser melting, can produce geometrically complex components.
Metal additive manufacturing can achieve excellent mechanical characteristics in several alloy classes, including high-entropy alloys.
Some powder-preparation routes can add processing complexity, expense, or feedstock-flow problems to additive manufacturing.
A comparative build study with and without multi-scale-modeling optimization can test the hypothesis.
Mechanical properties and residual thermal stresses will be measured in the comparative experiment.
The hypothesis is falsified if the mechanical-property improvement is less than 10%.
